nameStory: The Red-juice Tooth gets its name from its most striking feature - young mushrooms literally "bleed" bright red droplets that look like strawberry juice! This dramatic guttation process, where the fungus expels excess moisture through its pores, creates droplets so vivid they've earned it nicknames like "Devil's tooth" and "bleeding tooth fungus." The "tooth" part comes from the spiny, tooth-like projections underneath that release spores.
description: The Red-juice Tooth is one of New England's most bizarre-looking fungi, appearing like a white cushion dotted with drops of bright red blood. When young and fresh, these mushrooms have irregular, bumpy white caps that can range from small buttons to hand-sized specimens. They belong to the "tooth fungi" group, meaning they produce spores on hanging spines underneath rather than gills or pores. As they age, they lose their dramatic red bleeding and turn brown and unremarkable.

idTips.label: Red Droplets
idTips.description: Young specimens "bleed" bright red droplets that bead up on the white surface like drops of strawberry syrup. These droplets are sticky to the touch and stain fingers red.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Irregular, bumpy white surface when young, often with multiple caps fused together. Feels firm and somewhat velvety, with a white margin that stays clean-looking.

idTips.label: Spore Surface
idTips.description: Underneath, hanging tooth-like spines replace gills or pores. These spines are white to pinkish and feel slightly soft when fresh.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Short, thick, and often irregular or barely visible, colored similar to the cap. Multiple stems may fuse together at the base.

idTips.label: Aging Changes
idTips.description: Older specimens lose the red droplets entirely and turn brown, crusty, and hard to the touch, becoming nearly unrecognizable.

idTips.label: Safety Note
idTips.description: Considered inedible and potentially bitter-tasting. Never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification, especially unusual-looking species like this one.

habitat: Look for Red-juice Tooth growing directly from soil in coniferous forests, particularly around pine, spruce, and fir trees. They form partnerships with tree roots (mycorrhizal relationships) and prefer acidic, well-drained forest soils. You'll find them scattered individually or in small groups, sometimes with multiple fruiting bodies fused together into larger masses.

seasonality.spring: Rarely fruiting in late spring, but any specimens found will be past their prime and brown. Look for last year's dried, crusty remains still attached to the forest floor.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season begins in mid to late summer, especially after periods of rain. Fresh specimens with bright red droplets are most likely to be found during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Prime season continues through early fall when most specimens with active red bleeding can be observed. Later fall specimens may start losing their droplets and begin browning.
seasonality.winter: No active fruiting, but old, dried brown specimens may persist under snow cover and can be found during winter thaws as hard, woody remnants.

funFact: Those red droplets aren't just for show - they contain a natural blood thinner called atromentin that works similarly to the medical drug heparin, making this humble forest fungus a potential source of anticoagulant compounds!
confusionNotes: When the red droplets are absent, brown aged specimens can be confused with other tooth fungi, but the Red-juice Tooth's irregular, often fused growth pattern and preference for coniferous forests helps distinguish it. Memory trick: if it's not actively "bleeding" red and looks boring, it's probably too old to identify with certainty or might be a different tooth fungus entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its alarming "bleeding" appearance, this fungus is completely harmless to humans and actually beneficial to forest ecosystems. The dramatic visual display is simply the mushroom's way of managing excess water, not a sign of injury or decay.
compareHints: Among its tooth fungus relatives, Red-juice Tooth is the only one that produces bright red droplets when young. The Zoned Tooth shows concentric color bands, while the Blue Tooth has bluish tints, but neither "bleeds" red liquid. Orange Rough-cap Tooth has orange coloring but lacks the dramatic guttation droplets that make Red-juice Tooth unmistakable when fresh.
